The Manosphere Isn’t Ready for Brothercore

📅 21 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 20 min read (4076 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: WIRED

⏱️ ~20 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • On a sweltering July morning, in the middle of an empty playground in suburban Denver, two extremely fit, sweaty, shirtless male influencers are tussling in the dirt.
  • “The guy on top who’s in control, we call that position riding,” one of the grapplers, Carlos Monteon Jr.
  • According to recent reports, monteon and Cole continue scuffling.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

On a sweltering July morning, in the middle of an empty playground in suburban Denver, two extremely fit, sweaty, shirtless male influencers are tussling in the dirt.

“The guy on top who’s in control, we call that position riding,” one of the grapplers, Carlos Monteon Jr. pauses to explain to a group of eight similarly fit, sweaty, nearly all shirtless men who are watching the action in a circle. Monteon is a wrestler and influencer from Arizona, with pomelo-sized biceps, glossy shoulder-length hair, and more than 675,000 followers across TikTok and Instagram. He turns to his demo partner, Johnny Cole, a rangy, then 28-year-old content creator (59,000 TikTok followers) with a penchant for slutty tank tops. “And this one is called the Saturday night ride.”.

According to recent reports, monteon and Cole continue scuffling. The match ends with Monteon straddling Cole, their faces inches apart, their torsos glistening. The scene looks like a JV wrestling match.

The other men pair up to take turns grappling. Two cameramen circle them as a drone hums overhead.

“Yes, testosterone!” one influencer yells.

According to recent reports, “And estrogen!” Cole adds. “Both of them together, as one!”.

In a recent development, I’m at Hey Brother House, a content incubator that hosts weeklong retreats for male social media influencers. The organization teaches men and boys “to embody healthy masculinity, fully process emotions, embrace authenticity, and show up as compassionate, empathetic community leaders,” according to its website.

Filmmaker Vince Nett captures the shirtless shenanigans of Carlos Monteon Jr.

According to recent reports, cole, the founder of Hey Brother, helms the project with two other house leaders. Jonathan Jacobs, an affable 37-year-old who owns a digital marketing agency in Los Angeles, is wearing a brown cap that says “Male Friendship.” Matthew Echelman, a 35-year-old Brooklyn-based filmmaker, has hired two crew members to film the whole thing for a possible future documentary. Funded by a grant of more than $180,000 from an initiative called the Young Men and Media Collective, Hey Brother House’s goal is to flood 18-to-25-year-old men’s social media feeds with content that will (hopefully) make them less terrible.

The house itself is a rented stucco McMansion next to the Green Valley Ranch Golf Club, a residential community just outside Denver. In some respects, it looks like your average fratty domicile: There’s a Nintendo Switch console in the living room, where the boys play Mario Kart; a basement decked out with fitness equipment, a sauna, air hockey, and Foosball; and a makeshift indoor putting green. But there’s also a strict house alcohol ban, remote-controlled bidets, a box of wigs, swag boxes filled with fuchsia “Redefining Masculinity” T-shirts, and a wall covered in Post-Its of “gifts” the men can give each other, including “laying down on couch or blanket in park with my head on your lap.” There’s even a room—the “Man Box”—for testimonials, where the “cast members” can speak directly to the camera about their day. It’s reminiscent of reality TV, except most everyone is aware of bell hooks’ All About Love: Newly introduced Visions, and they are explicitly here to make friends.

Recent findings suggest that these guys are all in Denver because, as Cole puts it while he smokes Marlboro Lights on the porch, “men and boys are not doing well. And they have not been doing well for a long time.” The evidence supporting this is manifold: Young men are less likely than their female counterparts to finish high school and then enroll in college. They’re dropping out of the job market, and they’re more likely to report loneliness and isolation, as well as more likely to die by suicide.

Part of the problem is the manosphere, the social media ecosystem populated by looksmaxxers, incels, AI-touting hustle bros, and peptide-injecting fitness influencers. Initially a relatively fringe coalition, the “manosphere” has evolved into an online force to be reckoned with, thanks to the massive success of influencers like Jordan Peterson, a former academic who has advocated for all-meat diets and climate-change denialism; and, later, Andrew Tate, a failed kickboxer turned minor webcam impresario, who is presently facing more than 40 criminal charges in the UK and Romania, including trafficking and sex crimes. By preaching traditional masculinity as a path toward self-empowerment, so-called manosphere influencers have appealed to an audience of young men disillusioned by the rise of identity politics. Social media algorithms have happily amplified that message: By 2023, clips featuring Tate had more than 13 billion views on social media platforms.

Left to right: Jonathan Jacobs, Chris Petrone, and Johnny Cole collaborate on a social media house-tour video.

During the 2024 election, an estimated 67 percent of white male zoomers voted for Trump, resulting in a flurry of discourse about the manosphere’s power in channeling the frustrations of young men. “[They’ve] never had brotherhood or friendship,” Cole tells me. “They’ve never had another man look them in the eyes and say they’re worthy.” Men like Tate are successful, he notes, because they “weaponize this insecurity and this fragility and give them a scapegoat and say, ‘If you buy my course and you learn how to drop-ship, or come to my alphas-only elite men's circle, then you’ll become a high-value man.’”.

Of the three Hey Brother House leaders, Cole is the only one in the demographic the creators are trying to reach. He’s 6'4" and built like a varsity swimmer, with translucent green eyes, gray-painted nails, and light brown hair, which he dyes green and magenta for a short while after he leaves the house. He characterizes his work trying to reach young men as something akin to a divine calling.

Recent findings suggest that “I’m a white man who was a college rugby player, and I do jujitsu, but I also wear earrings and talk about feminism online,” he tells me. “Some of these guys think I’m performative, but in my experience, when I work with men and boys in person, they love me. They've never experienced a man who's a near peer who calls them into accountability, who offers them hugs and encouragement and support. In a looksmaxxing world, for these young guys I’m someone to look up to, literally and figuratively.”.

Sources indicate that this is where the Hey Brother House comes in: to teach progressive-leaning, male creators how to create content that captures the attention of the Kick-streaming, Zyn-sucking, butt-cut-sporting contingent. The goal is to adopt the visual hallmarks of the manosphere—slick editing, dynamic hooks, fast-paced montages—and apply those to what the house calls “healthy masculinity” content: dudes thrift-shopping together and picking out outfits, or guys playing golf while also wearing pink. “What we're not gonna do is stand in front of a camera, wag our fingers, and say, ‘I think that the patriarchy is the fucking worst thing in the world,’” Cole says.

Of course, there’s plenty of content for young men on social media that does not encourage men to become webcam pimps or forcefully hit themselves in the face with hammers, a la Clavicular. But much of the content in the “healthy masculinity” space is filled with academic jargon and feminist buzzwords. Or it’s more along the lines of Joe Rogan–infused, “Thunderdome-style” masculinity. (Think Instagram posts of white men with tribal tattoos weeping in the desert, with a caption promoting an online crypto investing class.) The Hey Brother House aims to teach male influencers how to promote values like empathy and vulnerability, via content about wrestling or fitness or style or financial advice. “It’s sugar with the medicine,” Cole claims.

An activity at the Hey Brother House where members offer gifts to the group and request actions they would like to receive from others.

In selecting the initial cohort for the Hey Brother House, Cole, Echelman, and Jacobs had to strike a delicate balance: They wanted creators who would be “mission-aligned,” as Jacobs put it, but who don’t exclusively make political content. Out of more than 130 applicants, they selected eight men. Some were leftist commentators like Jerry Zeng (133,000 Instagram followers), a 29-year-old, tatted, Jacquemus shorts-wearing video essayist from Houston, and Ian Lightfoot (1 million Instagram followers), an immaculately-eyebrowed, now 26-year-old whose Instagram bio proffers “positivity, popcorn, and bite-sized politics.” Others were more conventional lifestyle influencers like Sean Jones, a premed student who makes cute date-night videos and productivity vlogs, and the Houston-based trainer Stephen Marmolejos (180,000 TikTok followers), who posts fitness content and does sponcon for brands like Corona and Thayers. One, the artist and dancer Mars Wright (195,000 TikTok followers), is a trans man who has never lived in a house with cis men before. “I kind of feel like I’m entering the cafeteria scene in Mean Girls,” he told me before he got to Denver.

I arrive at the house from my hotel to find the guys midway through a vulnerability exercise in the living room. (For four days, I was given almost total access but was politely asked not to attend the first day of exercises, so the men could bond.).

According to recent reports, I quietly take a seat on a corduroy couch as the men stand in two parallel lines, facing their partners and taking turns answering the question: “What would you know if you really knew me?” All speaking at once, they say things like: “my father,” “my angry feelings,” “even my best relationship,” “Weight Watchers.” They are mic’d, and the cameras are out in full force, zooming in as the men embrace and thank each other for listening. Some are crying.

Later, the guys sit in a talking circle—one of many I would witness—and unpack their feelings. This is the first time some of them, particularly the brawnier health-and-fitness influencer types, have had such intimate conversations with other men, talking about their marriages, surviving domestic violence, trauma, addiction. “I started out with vague surface-level things that were quirky,” Monteon says afterward, “but at the very end I felt safe enough, and I revealed way more than I expected to.”.

Cole, who leads the exercise, nods empathetically. “You can’t heal if you don’t reveal,” he says, the men snapping in assent. (There is a lot of affirmative snapping at the house; there is also repeated use of terms like “aligned,” “affirmed,” and “container,” a reference to a therapeutic trauma-processing modality. I heard about containers a dozen times, only once in the context of a physical vessel.).

Industry observers note that the next morning, when I meet the guys for the first full day’s activity—a trip to a thrift store where the men select outfits for each other—approximately 40 percent of them are hungover from karaoke the night before, as well as the day of emotional disclosures. (As Zeng put it to me, “there’s been a lot of trauma-dumping.”) But they seem genuinely psyched for the activity, which is intended to culminate in filming a wholesome “dress your bro for a night out”–type video.

Journaling is a popular practice at the Hey Brother House.

“It’s a lot of pressure. I’ve never shopped for another dude, [or] heard a man compliment another man’s outfit,” Chris Petrone (1.6 million TikTok followers), tells me. “At first I was nervous, but then I was like, let’s get funky.” A baby-faced 31-year-old who lives in Florida, Petrone is one of the most successful creators in the Hey Brother House, thanks in part to a 2021 viral video in which he advocated for men to stock tampons in their bathrooms for female guests; for about a year, he had “the CEO of tampons” in his bio.

If they are nervous, they don’t show it. Monteon, who arrives in a Movember cap and brown sweats, leaves with jeans and a brown and white geometric-patterned button-down, looking like a 1970s Tiger Beat centerfold. And when Lightfoot tries on a purple and yellow cropped windbreaker, Wright and Josh Kennedy, a 29-year-old mustachioed, Wichita-based personal trainer, snap in assent. “That was literally made for you,” Kennedy claims.

The Hey Brother House was conceived, at least in part, as a content incubator. But aside from the documentary film crew being present for almost every activity, not a ton of content is actually being made. Occasionally, I turn a corner and see guys editing footage on a laptop or someone filming multiple takes of a house tour in the foyer.

According to recent reports, instead, the dudes seemed focused on … being dudes. They played Mario Kart and went for runs. They talked about what dog breeds they would be. “I am not a scary dog,” Jones stated. “And I do believe I am majestic at times.”.

Sources indicate that even Wright, who was initially anxious about living in a house with cis men—some of whom had never met a trans man before—promptly bonded with the other members. “I've always wanted to be in community with other men and feel like I belonged and like I was one of them,” he says. “And honestly, I didn’t really believe that a lot of men were having these conversations until I was behind closed doors with them.”.

Sources indicate that the bros are sitting in the living room for a content brainstorming session. They are watching a slew of manosphere clips, which Cole indicates embody the three “Rs” of masculinity: “relentlessly rich and ripped.” He then highlights a few examples of Reels that he identifies as “really brother-core coded”: a challenge video of men guessing the drinks that have been thrown in their faces, or tips for how men can protect their girlfriends from drink-spiking at bars. The goal, says Jacobs, is not to “attack the messenger” by making fun of Andrew Tate or Jordan Peterson because “that puts people on the defensive.” The men volley around a few ideas, which are similarly wholesome and tongue-in-cheek: golf cart racing, a parody of Jordan Peterson, rating each other’s hugs.

Then Wright pitches an idea for an “ask a trans person” video series, and the warm brotherly vibes start to shift. Wright prefaces his pitch by saying that, during his time in the house, a few of the other members had unintentionally “asked him questions that you should never ask a trans person.” Though he doesn’t name names or call anyone out specifically, he proposes that the snafu serves as a teaching moment for cisgender men watching Hey Brother House content.

According to recent reports, “Trans people don’t believe that any cis men care about them at all,” Wright says. “I want to show my community that there are men who care for them and would stand up for them and would be willing to be put in a situation that makes them a little uncomfortable.”.

Many of the guys are on board, but Cole visibly bristles at the suggestion, saying the idea causes him “reservation [and] anxiety” due to the possibility of it generating backlash from LGBTQ viewers.

The group holds a meeting to talk through a conflict that has caused tension. Facing camera, left to right: Chris Petrone and Johnny Cole. Facing away, from left to right: Ian Lightfoot and Jerry Zeng.

Industry observers note that “I wasn’t worried about being canceled,” he tells me later. “I was worried about the emotional and energetic impact of that series when we, as a container of men, had not addressed the emotional and energetic impact of things that had been mentioned offline.” But this wasn’t how Wright interpreted it. “I was really shocked he reacted like that,” he states. “He’s one of the few cis men to say that trans people really belong, and he invited me here, which was a dream come true. And it’s so gut-wrenchingly painful to see somebody react to you like, ‘Well, I don’t know how this is going to make me look.’”.

The impact of the conflict doesn’t become clear until the next day, when members of the House are abruptly summoned upstairs for a “tribunal.”.

In a recent development, the vibes are off almost immediately. The House members clearly have no idea what the purpose of the meeting is and are even more flummoxed when one of the camera crew members asks them to head back down and come up again, so they can get a better take. They sit in a circle, baffled, as Echelman, not Cole, opens the meeting by reading a seven-minute statement off his iPhone. Echelman, the documentarian, has largely been absent from the House activities. He occasionally chimes in during meetings and with video pitches during the brainstorm, including “a haunted house, but the ghosts are subverting gender expectations.”.

In a recent development, “In line with safety and consent, some things have arisen over the course of the house around conflict that I think it's important to not shy away from, but welcome and embrace and talk through,” he reads. “Rather than let that pass quietly, we want to name how we hold conflict here. Conflict isn't a failure of this space. It's where we practice communication, accountability, and care. And holding space means letting someone name their experience without filtering it.” Then Echelman opens the floor for questions.

On the third floor, the day after the tense emotional group meeting, all that remains is a box of tissues.

Immediately, someone states that they’re confused. “I echo that sentiment,” Cole says. “Are there things that you would like to name that you have observed in this space which prompted you to write that and call this meeting?”.

In a recent development, echelman’s explanation lasts an additional five minutes, over the course of which two things gradually become clear to everyone present: (1) this meeting is about Cole, and (2) he had no idea. Echelman accuses Cole of unintentionally abusing his leadership position to shut people down, and he brings up a critique raised by one house member that the “dress your bro” thrifting activity could be perceived on social media as “poverty porn” or depriving resources from low-income communities. (Echelman’s own “haunted house for toxic masculinity” pitch is not specifically mentioned.) “In a leadership position, it's our responsibility to, even if we’re feeling something in the moment, not to make it about us but someone else being so vulnerable and opening up to us,” he claims.

The tribunal, several house members told me afterward, was a disaster. As the men splinter off to go rock-climbing or golfing, Lightfoot tells me, “It felt less like an authentic conversation and more like a reality TV show.” A visibly upset Wright says he had confronted Cole privately about the brainstorm and specifically told Echelman that he did not want to have a meeting in front of the cameras with the group about what happened. To hear him tell it, he was less angry than disappointed. “Their hearts are in the right place,” he says of the House leaders. “They’re working tooth and nail, day and night, to make a difference. But we’re still so far from where we need to be.”.

Later, Echelman will dispute others’ characterization of the tribunal: “Plenty of people after the conversation stated that we broke the glass ceiling, because we could finally be open and honest with one another,” he tells me later.

Recent findings suggest that he isn’t entirely wrong. After the initial confrontation with Cole, some of the men brought up their own minor conflicts from Hey Brother House. Without exception, they had been addressed graciously and without grandstanding. There was no bluster for the cameras, no aggression, no dick-measuring; none of what you would come to expect from a group of men in conflict with each other. They listened. They affirmed. They told each other how grateful they were for the experience of being there together. Even if the house leaders were in conflict, the creators themselves were “synced up completely,” Wright tells me. “I look at any one of them, and I know they would make me feel safe and comfortable.” It didn’t necessarily make for compelling content, but it did seem like they had taken Cole’s earlier lesson to heart: you can’t heal if you don’t reveal. (Snaps).

Josh Kennedy (left) and Johnny Cole have a heartfelt conversation while doing the dishes.

Cole, Echelman, and Jacobs are now selecting the cohort for the next House, which will take place in Austin in December, followed by a third in Atlanta. Nearly all eight are already confirmed, including leftist bodybuilder Colin Davis and trans former NCAA athlete Schuyler Bailar. The leaders have apparently hashed things out and are working to correct some of the mistakes they made with the Denver House, enlisting the services of an in-person, trained men’s group facilitator to mediate conflicts. “This is a test-and-learn pilot,” Jacobs tells me. “While we are comfortable with swings and misses, we also want to ensure we don’t keep taking the same swing.” Cole’s friend, whom he describes as a “professional race car driver and videographer,” will also be on hand to record social media content. “He's 22 and has a really vibey aesthetic,” he says. “He knows what's t-u-f-f, tuff.”.

In a recent development, all told, the creators at the Hey Brother House produced somewhere between 65 and 70 videos. The main focus was on bonding activities and group discussions. The highest-performing video was a clip of Wright injecting himself with testosterone as the other men cheered him on, which got 689,000 views. After the tribunal, the House also produced his “Ask a Trans Man” video series, which overperformed on both Instagram and Wright’s YouTube channel; in one, Cole and Wright, who have since made up, were prominently featured.

Little of the content from Hey Brother House went viral, but for a handful of the creators, their audience now skews more male; Wright, for instance, says some of his content from the house reached a predominantly male audience. But in reaching their target demo—men from 18 to 25—they saw little success. “There are some ways in which our content was too on the nose,” says Cole. In the future, he says they’ll make more of “the type of stuff that young men want to see” — such as the wrestling videos, which he says overperformed. For this reason, they’re trying to recruit a much younger cohort for Austin, who focus less on political commentary and more on skits and lifestyle content. They’re having some difficulty: many younger male creators often have to juggle their content creation with school. A lot of them have talent managers who don’t want their clients to “get too political,” or have turned down the House because they can’t pay them that much.

Josh Kennedy (left) cheers on Johnny Cole and Ian Lightfoot as they hug after their dance-off performances at The Movement Project.

Sources indicate that but there are signs pointing in the direction of a healthier version of manhood being promoted on social media—or, at the very least, an exhaustion with older models. Following the midterm elections in November, men like senators-elect Abdul El-Sayed, James Talarico, and Sen. Jon Ossoff emerged triumphant at the polls, proffering a kindler and gentler (not to mention hunkier) model of masculinity than any proffered by a Clavicular or an Androgenic. Perhaps even more tellingly, white men between the ages of 18 and 29, who had previously helped deliver the 2024 election to Trump, swung overwhelmingly left. According to one analysis, 54 percent of this bracket voted for Democratic House candidates.

Recent findings suggest that there was also one video that came out of Denver that did indeed perform well with the target demographic of Gen Z men. A simple, five-second looping Instagram Reel reveals Kennedy and Cole locked in an embrace. “When’s the last time you got a hug longer than 5 seconds?” the onscreen text reads. It has garnered 500,000 views, mostly from 18-to-24-year-olds.

I am reminded of something Cole told me the first time we spoke about how to solve the toxic masculinity crisis. “I know so strongly in my soul that more men and boys just need more hugs,” he said. “No matter what you’ve been through, no matter who you are. You just need more hugs [and] safe touches and affirmation and encouragement.” At the time, this struck me as cringe, and maybe a bit too simplistic. Watching the Reel with Kennedy and Cole embracing, I feel the same. But that doesn’t mean it’s not also true.

Anthropic researcher uses AI to solve math's greatest riddle

📅 21 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 2 min read (461 words, 📖 Standard) | Source: Dw

⏱️ ~2 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • A mathematician working for AI giant Anthropic says he used the firm's Claude AI tool to solve one of mathematics most famous problems.
  • The Riemann hypothesis dates back to 1859 and centers on the distribution of prime numbers underpinning a much wider scope of mathematical work.
  • Levent Alpoge, a member of Anthropic's technical staff, made the announcement on his website.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

A mathematician working for AI giant Anthropic says he used the firm's Claude AI tool to solve one of mathematics most famous problems.

The Riemann hypothesis dates back to 1859 and centers on the distribution of prime numbers underpinning a much wider scope of mathematical work.

Levent Alpoge, a member of Anthropic's technical staff, made the announcement on his website. "I believe I have, working with Claude, discovered a proof of the Riemann Hypothesis," Levent Alpoge wrote in a note released Friday.

It has been revealed that the proof still has to be verified and confirmed by other mathematicians. If it withstands independent examination, it would be a major milestone both in mathematics and the growing role of artificial intelligence (AI) in scientific research.

The Riemann hypothesis is the latest and most key in a string of famous mathematical problems that were tackled with the help of AI.

Alpoge said that the collaboration with AI had generated more than 250,000 pages of mathematical material, adding that he had not yet mastered all the mathematics involved.

"Claude and I have had a great time together with such breadth in recent months, but this time Claude far outpaced me near the finish line," he wrote. "No, Claude flew, and danced, and sparkled near that finish line.".

The Riemann Hypothesis is one of seven major mathematical problems, the so-called Millennium Prize Problems, selected by the Clay Mathematics Institute, which offers $1 million for a solution to each of those.

"This is an announcement of historic significance," Martin Bridson, president of the institute, stated in a statement quoted by news agency AP.

He added it "holds the promise of a dramatic transformation in the perception of what is possible in the struggle to extend the human understanding of mathematics.".

"But the journey from today’s announcement to a place of real understanding will be long and difficult.".

Formulated by German mathematician Bernhard Riemann in the 19th century, the hypothesis is about the distribution of prime numbers, which are numbers that can only be divided by themselves and the number 1.

The hypothesis describes a fundamental pattern of how these numbers are distributed as they become ever larger. Confirming that hypothesis is thought to have crucial implications for a wide range of further mathematical research.

The potential breakthrough by Alpoge and Claude AI comes amid a growing number of examples where artificial intelligence systems are making significant contributions to advanced mathematical research.

In September, rival AI manufacturer OpenAI noted its technology had helped solve a problem involving the Navier-Stokes equations.

The equations, which describe the movement of fluids such as water and air, are another of the seven Millennium Prize Problems, but the claim that they've been solved also still needs independent verification.

#47446. Latest Update: A human liver has been kept alive outside the body for a record seven weeks

Latest Update: A human liver has been kept alive outside the body for a record seven weeks

📅 19 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (1041 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Technologyreview

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Researchers in Australia claim they’ve kept a human liver alive, on life support, outside the body for seven weeks, opening up speculative new possibilities in biomedical engineering.
  • The feat, whose details are pending publication, was carried out in Sydney after a team led by surgeon and inventor Carlo Pulitano connected a donated liver to a system of automated pumps and sensors that fed the organ nutrients, supplied it with blood, and whisked away waste.
  • In an interview, Pulitano, a transplant surgeon at the Royal Prince Alfred Hospital and a professor at the University of Sydney, likened the life support system to “an artificial body.” Its official name is the Extended Organ Perfusion System.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Researchers in Australia claim they’ve kept a human liver alive, on life support, outside the body for seven weeks, opening up speculative new possibilities in biomedical engineering.

The feat, whose details are pending publication, was carried out in Sydney after a team led by surgeon and inventor Carlo Pulitano connected a donated liver to a system of automated pumps and sensors that fed the organ nutrients, supplied it with blood, and whisked away waste.

In an interview, Pulitano, a transplant surgeon at the Royal Prince Alfred Hospital and a professor at the University of Sydney, likened the life support system to “an artificial body.” Its official name is the Extended Organ Perfusion System.

“Our group is the only one in the world to have maintained a human liver under fully normothermic, physiological conditions for seven weeks,” he indicates.

Industry observers note that normothermic means body temperature, or about 37 °C. The previous record for keeping an internal organ alive outside the body was set in Switzerland several years ago. That organ—also a liver—lasted around two weeks.

Most organs destined for transplant survive only a few hours in special ice buckets and need to be raced to their destination. Over the last decade, however, surgeons have been switching to perfusion systems, which pump warm or cold fluids into an organ. This can double the time it can be held before it must be transplanted.

Sources indicate that pulitano states the key to breaking the record was to automate the systems used to keep the organ thriving. During a meeting in Switzerland earlier this year, the Sydney team described perfusing 55 human livers, one after the other. Some were connected to a system that needed to be adjusted manually, but for those placed on the automated system—which produced the seven-week survivor—the average survival time tripled, to about four weeks.

Industry observers note that perfusion has already enabled doctors to restart hearts from dead people and keep them beating outside the body. Paulo Martins, a transplant doctor at the University of Oklahoma, states about half the kidneys he transplants are now perfused, even though the process can add $100,000 to the cost of a transplant.

While the research awaits formal publication, the eventual goal is what Pulitano and colleagues call “time-unlimited liver preservation.”.

Sources indicate that scientists have already discovered possible medical benefits to keeping organs on life support longer than usual. One, they say, is that perfused organs apparently start to repair themselves and become stronger after a day or so. That’s what led a Swiss team, in 2022, to transplant a damaged liver that had been kept on perfusion for three days—the longest time any internal organ had remained outside the body before a successful transplant, claims Waldemar Hoffmann, the CEO and cofounder of Apersys, a startup formed to commercialize the technology.

Pulitano indicates his own startup, Aeternum Life Technologies, will be helping with a planned trial in Sydney to transplant low-quality livers kept on perfusion for four days.

What’s less clear, says Hoffmann, is whether any transplant surgeon would ever want, or need, to use an organ kept alive for nearly two months. He says people in the field believe Pulitano’s record is real, but they don’t know how healthy the organ was at the end or even what so much extra time is likely to achieve. “The key question is what the purpose for a seven-week perfusion would be,” he says.

Yet that’s where things could start to get interesting, says Martins, the Oklahoma surgeon. Long-term life support could enable far-out concepts like artificial wombs, new types of organ manufacturing, and the chance to experiment directly on human organs outside the body for extended periods.

Sources indicate that for his part, Pulitano notes long-term machine perfusion could help grow upcoming organs. In living donations, surgeons commonly take half of a person’s liver to give someone else. After about two months, both parts will have grown back almost to their full volume. Pulitano says he’s tried dividing a liver and then attaching the sections to the machine. If that works, he says, it could be a way to multiply one donor liver into several full-size organs.

In a recent development, “It’s crucial to have people thinking outside the box and pushing the limits and creating possibilities for things that, right now, sometimes we don’t even have a need for but are going to be needed in the future,” indicates Martins. “That’s how science moves.”.

According to recent reports, he’s not the only one who thinks so. For instance, a US company, Bexorg, has been reanimating human brains using perfusion pumps. The idea is to study what effects experimental drugs have on them. That company perfuses brains for about a day but has noted it wants to extend the time to two weeks.

Similar experiments can be done on livers, states Pulitano, who has already tried adding gene therapies to the organs. “It gives us a living human organ model for translational research that no animal system can match, because the biology, the immunology, and the drug responses are human from the outset,” he says.

It has been revealed that meanwhile, in Silicon Valley, patents filed by Altos Labs, a billionaire-backed longevity startup, describe attempts to introduce reprogramming genes into animal livers maintained outside the body. Eventually, Altos scientists have speculated, they might temporarily disconnect a failing organ while it’s still in a person’s body, connecting it to a perfusion machine in order to douse it with ultra-powerful genetic treatments without risking the rest of the body.

Doctors probing the limits of organ life support have now formed two new scientific societies to explore the concept. One, founded by Martins and called the International Society for Organ Preservation and Perfusion Therapy, will hold its inaugural meeting this year in Italy. The other, based in China, was launched in August to advance what doctors at the First Affiliated Hospital of Sun Yat-Sen University have termed “organ medicine”: research at the level of whole organs kept alive by “bionic maintenance.”.

Industry observers note that “What is exploding is the idea of this technology that clearly goes beyond simply organ preservation,” indicates Pulitano. “Basically, that’s a concept that’s entirely newly introduced.”.

Tech Report: Rocket Report: A weekend of ups and downs; Stoke celebrates engine milestone

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Welcome to Edition 9.20 of the Rocket Report!
  • Industry observers note that europe’s leading satellite startup eyes Italian rocket maker.
  • Sources indicate that fulfilling a need … In a statement, ICEYE mentioned it wants to join forces with Avio to meet Europe’s need for “sovereign space and defense capabilities.” ICEYE manufactures and operates its own satellites for radar surveillance and sells data to commercial customers and national governments, including Ukraine, which uses ICEYE imagery for targeting and tracking Russian troop movements.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Welcome to Edition 9.20 of the Rocket Report! Last weekend was a picture of the US launch business in miniature, and emblematic of the opposing trajectories of two of the nation’s most experienced rocket makers. First, on Saturday, SpaceX completed a perfect midair catch of its Starship upper stage at its launch pad in Texas after spending nearly a day in orbit. The Super Heavy booster was lost at sea, but SpaceX proved it can recover that piece of the rocket on previous flights. While SpaceX demonstrated it is well on the way to fielding a fully reusable rocket, United Launch Alliance suffered its first-ever total launch failure with the Vulcan rocket. That is terrible news for not only ULA, but also the US Space Force and Amazon, which have booked some 70 debuts on Vulcan over the next few years. Your faithful correspondents will take a break from the Rocket Report next week for the Thanksgiving holiday, so we’ll see you again the first week of December.

Industry observers note that europe’s leading satellite startup eyes Italian rocket maker. Finnish satellite developer ICEYE confirmed Tuesday that it is seeking to buy Italian rocket-maker Avio for more than $2.2 billion in a transaction aimed at creating Europe’s first true vertically integrated end-to-end space company, Ars reports. Avio builds the Vega C rocket, a solid-fueled launcher designed to carry up to 3.3 metric tons (7,300 pounds) of payload to low-Earth orbit. ICEYE is, by far, the most successful space startup in Europe, with a valuation of more than $12 billion after the company’s most recent fundraising round in June.

Sources indicate that fulfilling a need … In a statement, ICEYE mentioned it wants to join forces with Avio to meet Europe’s need for “sovereign space and defense capabilities.” ICEYE manufactures and operates its own satellites for radar surveillance and sells data to commercial customers and national governments, including Ukraine, which uses ICEYE imagery for targeting and tracking Russian troop movements. Most of ICEYE’s satellites have rolled out on SpaceX Falcon 9 rockets. With Falcon 9’s retirement on the horizon, ICEYE’s satellites will need rides to orbit. Avio’s Vega C rocket has a healthy backlog of contracts for European governments, but it hasn’t been a hit commercially. Investment from ICEYE could shore up Avio’s Vega rocket program and perhaps accelerate development of a latest rocket.

NATO unveils launch brokerage initiative. The North Atlantic Treaty Organization is contracting commercial rockets and spaceports to grow its satellite launch network and help neutralize risks to the space systems on which it relies, Bloomberg reports. NATO launched two initiatives on Tuesday: Starlift, through which participating countries can secure slots on commercial rockets, and the Global Data Marketplace, which will bolster the alliance’s military operations in space with commercial data and services.

It has been revealed that swimming in launches … Starlift will allow participating countries—Belgium, Canada, Finland, Germany, Italy, the Netherlands, Norway, Sweden, Turkey, the UK, and South Korea—to pool their military launch requirements and secure launch slots on commercial rockets. The NATO initiative will also prepare and test procedures for short-notice launches, as might be needed in a crisis. Bloomberg reported NATO’s tech agency will offer about $2.7 billion in contracts over the next two years, including to commercial space companies, AI, cyber, and command-and-control networks.

Stoke wraps up booster engine development. Stoke Space has completed development of its Zenith engine, the methane-fueled powerplant that will propel the manufacturer’s medium-class Nova rocket off the launch pad. Stoke made the announcement in a social media post Thursday. “As flight engines clear acceptance testing, we’re shipping them down to Cape Canaveral for integration with Nova’s first stage—every week,” Stoke said. Seven Zenith engines will power the Nova rocket’s reusable first stage booster, combining to generate about 700,000 pounds of thrust at full throttle.

According to recent reports, all eyes on Stage 2 … Stoke confirmed it cleared a “proto-qualification” milestone on Stage 1 earlier this year. Stage 2 is undergoing cryogenic proof testing and a hot-fire test campaign at Stoke’s test complex in rural Washington. Nova’s second stage is the real innovation, with a unique arrangement of 24 thrusters surrounding a regeneratively cooled heat shield to protect it during reentry back into Earth’s atmosphere. With this, Stoke aims to fully reuse both Nova stages. The first launch is presently expected sometime next year.

Soyuz flies from Russia’s Far East. A Soyuz-2.1b rocket made its first and only launch from Russia’s Vostochny Cosmodrome this year, RussianSpaceWeb.com reports. The rocket’s Fregat upper stage deployed a new pair of high-resolution imaging satellites, along with a cluster of smaller payloads, following liftoff from Russia’s Vostochny launch base on November 14 (local time). Vostochny, located in Russia’s Far East, hosted its first space launch in 2016. By some measures, Russia spent more than $5 billion building Vostochny, only to use it for an average of two launches per year.

Sources indicate that what was onboard? … Soyuz and Fregat carried two dual-use imaging surveillance satellites. A pair of CubeSat-class satellites for a Russian arms manufacturer were also onboard. These satellites are owned by NPO Kaisant, which specializes in drone communications and counter-drone weapons. NPO Kaisant indicates the satellites will join a constellation providing secure communications to Russian drones over Ukraine. A total of 12 secondary payloads were reported to be onboard, according to Roscosmos.

Recent findings suggest that china’s LandSpace reports rocket reuse milestone. Three months after landing its first orbital-class rocket booster, Chinese rocket tech giant LandSpace claims it has completed “ground acceptance and testing” of the nine methane-fueled engines recovered from the first stage of its Zhuque-3 rocket, according to Guandian News, a Chinese outlet focusing on the country’s financial and economic sector. The engines were disassembled, inspected, refurbished, reassembled, and retested after flying to space and back in August.

But wait … LandSpace’s Zhuque-3 is one of two Chinese rockets to successfully land its booster after an orbital launch attempt. The manufacturer did not say whether any of the nine engines will fly again, but don’t count on the entire Zhuque-3 booster stage from the August flight making another trip to space. The Zhuque-3 first stage toppled over soon after a seemingly flawless touchdown at LandSpace’s downrange recovery zone in northwestern China. Based on this week’s news, it appears engineers were able to salvage the engines.

According to recent reports, spaceX makes a historic catch. SpaceX, nearly a quarter of a century after its founding, took a hugely significant step toward developing and optimizing a massive, rapidly reusable rocket with the first successful catch of its enormous Starship upper stage on November 14, Ars reports. It’s hard to overstate the significance of the moment. SpaceX’s ability to recover and swiftly relaunch Starships and Super Heavy boosters is central to all of the company’s lofty commercial ambitions and many of America’s high-level strategic imperatives, from national security to maintaining dominance in space exploration.

What was it like to be there? … Ars Space Editor Eric Berger covered the launch and catch of Starship from a nearby perch at Starbase, Texas. “Watching Starship launch from here a little less than a day earlier, and knowing it had orbited the planet multiple times, added to the sense of unreality in seeing this spaceship return to Earth under its own power and be captured by the tower,” Berger writes. “It felt like stepping into the future. SpaceX has dazzled us before by landing rockets on barges and returning humans to space with Crew Dragon. But this flight took things to another level. Starships are huge. They carry a huge amount of energy coming back from orbit. And until a few years ago, it seemed beyond fantastical to think about capturing a rocket with what are essentially outsized chopsticks. Nevertheless, it happened.”.

Recent findings suggest that vulcan fails to deliver for Amazon. United Launch Alliance’s Vulcan rocket and 40 Amazon Leo broadband satellites fell back to Earth minutes after liftoff Sunday, a crushing setback that will ripple across all sectors of the US space industry, Ars reports. Aside from ULA itself, the fallout from the failure will strike the US military and Amazon hardest. Sunday’s mission was the first of 38 Vulcan introduces booked by Amazon to build out its network of broadband Internet satellites aimed at competing with SpaceX’s Starlink. Vulcan is also on contract to launch roughly half of the US Space Force’s national security missions over the next few years.

Identifying the cause … ULA stated Wednesday that the failure was caused by inadequate fuel supply to the first stage engines, Ars reports in a follow-up story. “ULA has completed an initial integrated review of flight data from the Leo 1 launch anomaly that occurred last Sunday,” the organization said in a statement. “While work remains to determine cause, preliminary indications are that the low booster thrust was the result of inadequate fuel supply from the vehicle to the BE-4 engines, not from the performance of the engines.” This is fantastic news for Blue Origin, which builds the BE-4 and uses a similar design on its own Latest Glenn rocket. Vulcan’s solid rocket boosters also performed as expected Sunday after experiencing nozzle failures on two prior Vulcan flights.

Google taps Blue Origin for AI launch. Blue Origin declared Thursday that its Fresh Glenn rocket will launch data center satellites for Google in 2029 as part of that company’s Project Suncatcher program, Ars reports. Google disclosed it was working on scalable orbiting data centers about a year ago and characterized the project as one of its research “moonshots.” The mission on New Glenn is designed to deploy satellites, each with computing capacity at roughly the scale of a data center rack, into Sun-synchronous orbit where they can receive nearly continuous solar energy.

Hitching a ride … Google snatched up a ride on Newly introduced Glenn just as US commercial heavy-lift rockets are filling up their capacity through the year 2030. The Google mission will fly on the 7×2 variant of the New Glenn rocket, the smaller version of the vehicle that has launched three times to date. The purpose of the 2029 launch will likely be to test the ability to network solar-powered satellites equipped with AI chips and demonstrate machine-learning compute in space. Perhaps the bigger question for Google is not whether it can make this technology work—but whether it is tenable for a company to have ambitions for a large constellation of orbital data centers in the 2030s without its own launch vehicle.

In a recent development, relativity makes progress with Terran R. Another newly introduced rocket is moving closer to the launch pad. Relativity Space’s partially reusable Terran R rocket could launch sometime next year if engineers can finish development with no major setbacks. Relativity posted an update on YouTube this week, detailing several recent achievements at several of the organization’s locations across the country. At Relativity headquarters in Southern California, teams have completed Terran R’s first stage thrust structure with a full set of 13 Aeon engines, fluid lines, and avionics. The engine compartment is now being integrated with Stage 1 tankage. Terran R’s second stage recently completed its first all-up test firing at Stennis Space Center, Mississippi.

It has been revealed that meanwhile, at Cape Canaveral … Relativity is also moving forward with the Terran R launch pad at Cape Canaveral Space Force Station, Florida. The launch pad’s lightning protection towers are now complete, as is the steel framing for Terran R’s launch table. Work continues on the rocket’s transporter-erector, strongback, and the launch pad’s propellant storage tanks.

November 20: Long March 8A | SatNet LEO Group | Wenchang Space Launch Site, China | 11:59 UTC.

November 21: Falcon 9 | USSF-317 | Vandenberg Space Force Base, California | 02:32 UTC.

November 21: Long March 6C | Unknown Payload | Taiyuan Satellite Launch Center, China | 03:50 UTC.

If your giftee is more of a sweatshirt gal, you also can't go wrong with the Fisherman Pullover Hoodie ($120) or the Full-Zip Hoodie ($120).

Everyone and their mother has an LED mask these days. If the woman in your life doesn’t, congratulations: You’ve found her gift. Chances are the Shark CryoGlow LED Face Mask is already on her wishlist. And if it isn't, she simply hasn’t done enough research. The CryoGlow delivers red, infrared, and blue light, which is everything your face could possibly need short of a dermatologist. Its preset routines live on an attached controller, so there’s no troubleshooting. The real selling point, though, is the under-eye cooling pads, which help reduce puffiness and add a therapeutic element to the experience. I gifted one to my mother, and now she has to actively defend it from her friends.

Industry observers note that get her the Eva Wearable Vibrator. A hands-free clitoral stimulation toy that can be used solo, but is best during penetrative sex. It’s tiny. It’s mighty. It’s hands-free (!!!), made of soft silicone, with three intensity levels. Gift the Eva to your best friend, or to your partner if you want to spice things up, in which case, you’re welcome.

Industry observers note that if I have to feed myself, I want a kitchen appliance that does most of my labor. The Breville Smart Oven Air Fryer Noir is that appliance. She’s goth. She’s gorgeous. She air-fries, slow-cooks, and bakes with zero complaints. There are 11 preset functions, to be exact. I don’t know what all of them do, and I don’t care, because she knows. I don’t want to think about settings, and with Breville’s Element iQ system, which auto-adjusts temperature for precision cooking, I don’t have to. There’s even an app, which I didn’t download because I’m busy. You can check out more of our Air Fryer picks here.

If she already owns an LED mask, it’s time to give her scalp the same VIP treatment. Red-light therapy isn’t just for pattern baldness; it may also help women experiencing all types of hair thinning and shedding, including postpartum hair loss. It can also help calm the scalp, increase blood flow, and regulate oil production. Reviewer Nena Farrell loves the HigherDose Red Light Hat, which is relatively affordable compared with competitors and looks like an ordinary baseball cap. That means she can take her self-care outside, and no one would ever know. How would they know?

If she’s training for a marathon, tracking her stress cycles, or just wants hard data to justify why she feels like garbage, the Oura Ring 5 is the most stylish health tracker out there. Packed with advanced sensors, it monitors heart rate, skin temperature, sleep quality, and stress levels. It's also one of the only wearables that can reliably predict my menstrual cycle. Plus, it works with both Android and iOS, so she’s not locked into a single tech ecosystem.

The BrüMate Togosa gets it. It’s a wine chiller, pitcher, or whatever you need it to be because we no longer have the patience for single-purpose objects. Slide in a prechilled bottle, twist the lid shut, and let the BevGuard triple insulation keep your drink icy without ice, condensation, or a watery demise. When the vibe shifts from pinot to sangria, swap out the chiller lid and pour in your batch of whatever (up to 49 ounces). The leakproof strainer lid also keeps fruit, ice, and other garnishes from pouring through. And because being checked out of Earth doesn’t mean trashing it, its lids are made from 13 recycled water bottles, some finishes are dishwasher-safe to conserve water usage, and the vessel itself is built to last a lifetime. (If for some reason it doesn’t, BrüMate also offers a lifetime warranty.).

Industry observers note that she may not be able to move to another planet, but she can build a 3D model of the Milky Way from the comfort of her home. This 3,000-ish piece LEGO set recreates the spiral galaxy, turning our jumbled universe into galactic home decor. The finished piece can be mounted on the wall as a daily reminder that Earth is just one of billions of planets we believe exist—surely, at least one of them has better men.

It has been revealed that the Everywhere Tote is for the woman who is going where the universe takes her. It has everything one might need for far-flung travels: a 16-inch padded laptop sleeve, a handful of interior pockets, and a water-resistant nylon exterior for when you’re caught in an otherworldly atmospheric anomaly. Available in elemental shades like coast blue, sea green, and clay pink—it’s at home anywhere, from the gym to an impromptu odyssey. If she needs to jet off on a moment’s notice, it’s got a key clip, a trolley sleeve, and an exterior pocket for her wallet and passport. It also meets airlines’ personal item requirements.

Sometimes, the only way to check out is to beam yourself into another world, preferably one with juicier plotlines. This projector has 450 ISO lumens and 1080p resolution, with 4K support and color calibration. The gimbal stand tilts 165 degrees for projecting on walls, ceilings, or the back of an RV. The included hard-shell case is great for portability and easy storage. It runs for 2.5 hours on a single charge, and it's power bank-compatible, so you can watch from anywhere. Its AI-powered setup takes care of autofocus, screen fit, obstacle avoidance, and keystone correction, so she doesn't have to fiddle with settings with every tectonic shake. For more projectors, check out our guide.

Cozy Earth’s Bamboo Pajama Set is one of my favorite sets to wear on a lazy Sunday. The button-up pocketed design features chic contrast piping that lends a hotel-style aesthetic. They make me want to put on my LED mask, pick up my Kindle, and sip on sleepy girl mocktails until I doze off. Made from 95 percent bamboo viscose and 5 percent spandex, this knit blend is cooler and more breathable than cotton. Cozy Earth introduces new colors and prints each season, though the lighter shades can be somewhat sheer. If your giftee is over 5 foot 7 inches, I recommend the tall inseam. Sizes range from XXS to XXXL.

These Speks Odds Silicone Fidget Magnets are here to help you survive your stay in the stress-stricken simulation. Each set comes with three palm-sized magnets, encased in soft, textured silicone, designed to keep your hands busy while your brain zones out. I can’t stop fiddling with them when I’m watching TV and during Zoom calls. I can’t risk losing them by taking them outside, so they’ve found a home on my desk.

Speks also sells starter kits and gift bundles packed with other fidget toys. I loved the Moon Jelly Gump Memory Gel Stress Ball, until I handed it to my boyfriend for five minutes and he popped it. Men ruin everything.

Walking home alone at night on this planet is an absolute nightmare. If she can’t teleport away from creeps, she can at least blast a 130-decibel siren and flashing strobe light in their direction. The Birdie is a small but mighty alarm that will (hopefully) deter attackers and alert anyone nearby for help.

It has been revealed that I’ve used the original model for over a year (see my thoughts in my guide to the Best Personal Safety Alarms), and it’s given me peace of mind whenever I’m walking solo. The Birdie+, which I have yet to test, adds some useful features like location sharing, emergency support, and even a fake call function for a quick exit strategy. Plus, it comes in the cutest patterns. My one caveat is that this wouldn't be my first choice for a birthday gift or Valentine's Day, as it's kind of a downer.

Sources indicate that she’s carrying her team at work, her family, and the knowledge that a recession is potentially looming. Don’t make her carry her water bottle, too. WanderFull’s Hydrobags have a thick, comfortable strap that takes a little bit of the load off her shoulders and come in dozens of colors and materials (including a latest clear stadium line), one of which is sure to match her vibe. All Hydrobags bags can hold any handle-less water bottle up to 11 inches tall and 3.5 inches in diameter and sport two pockets for her phone and cards. If you can’t redistribute the household labor, the least you could do is redistribute the weight of her emotional-support beverage. —Kat Merck.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Joshua Foster tells of moment he ‘lost control’ of two-year-old when he fell from fourth storey of hotel.
  • A British father who was fined by the courts after his two-year-old son fell from a fourth-floor window during a family holiday in Cyprus has recalled his “despair” when the boy slipped from his grasp.
  • Joshua Foster was handed a €3,000 (£2,500) penalty after he pleaded guilty to a charge of causing death through a reckless, rash or dangerous act.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Joshua Foster tells of moment he ‘lost control’ of two-year-old when he fell from fourth storey of hotel.

A British father who was fined by the courts after his two-year-old son fell from a fourth-floor window during a family holiday in Cyprus has recalled his “despair” when the boy slipped from his grasp.

Joshua Foster was handed a €3,000 (£2,500) penalty after he pleaded guilty to a charge of causing death through a reckless, rash or dangerous act. Prosecutors in Cyprus had refused to drop the case against him.

During recent court proceedings, it was heard that Foster thought the window at the King Evelthon Beach Hotel and Resort in Chlorakas was closed when he approached it with his son, Jaxon, to show him the view of a waterpark.

According to recent reports, the 37-year-old “lost control” of him, the Paphos district court was told, before the boy plunged 10 metres (33ft). The fall happened on 12 July, the first day of the Fosters’ family holiday.

Industry observers note that in an interview with the Daily Mail, Foster mentioned: “I have a burden. I’ll have that my whole life. It’s very traumatic. My mind doesn’t want to go there. I just remember the despair of him falling, and watching him fall.

“It was just such a shock … I put him up thinking he was going against a glass pane … and then he wasn’t there.”.

The toddler was pronounced dead at Paphos general hospital shortly after he suffered severe cranial injuries when he hit a veranda below.

Foster recalled his outpouring of emotion when he located his son after the fall. “I picked him up. I held him and screamed,” he stated. The Essex-born auditor said he and his wife had an hour with their son’s body after he was pronounced dead.

The decision to charge Foster, reported to be a senior accountant at KPMG, was criticised by his legal representatives, as well as human rights defenders, media pundits and diplomats, arguing that it lacked compassion.

Sources indicate that the charge Foster accepted is usually levelled in cases involving fatal traffic accidents. It carries a maximum penalty of four years in prison, but the fine he was handed was the lightest sentence possible for the offence.

At his sentencing in October, Judge Froso Christodoulidou ruled that Foster would not be jailed, before describing the incident as a “tragic event”.

The court had heard that, while the presence of alcohol had been detected in Foster’s blood, it was not enough to suggest he was impaired to the point where he had “acted recklessly”.

Industry observers note that foster was detained after the fall. He reportedly had to tell his eldest child, a daughter, about her brother’s death via a video call while he was being held.

He posted €30,000 (£26,000) in bail to return to the UK to attend the funeral of his son in August, but was forced, under threat of extradition, to return to Cyprus and surrender his passport by 14 September.

In a push for clemency, Foster’s legal team had appealed in September to the island’s attorney general, Cyprus’s top legal official, to discontinue the criminal procedure on humanitarian grounds. The request was denied.

Since returning home, Foster said the focus of his grieving family had turned to their daughter.

“It’s very difficult,” he said. “She waves at the sky and says: ‘I love you’ to him and blows a kiss. She’s lost her best friend. She’s gone from having a sibling to being an only child.”.

#47438. Why Apple Vision Pro never took off like Meta's VR headsets

Why Apple Vision Pro never took off like Meta's VR headsets

📅 21 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (871 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Engadget

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Good hardware doesn't necessarily make for a successful product.
  • When Apple launched the Vision Pro headset in early 2024, it was the most ambitious device the tech colossus had released in recent memory.
  • Recent findings suggest that but from our vantage point in 2026, it's clear the Vision Pro was doomed from the start.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Good hardware doesn't necessarily make for a successful product.

When Apple launched the Vision Pro headset in early 2024, it was the most ambitious device the tech colossus had released in recent memory. To find another device that so fundamentally wanted to change how we use tech, you'd probably have to go back to the original iPhone.

Recent findings suggest that but from our vantage point in 2026, it's clear the Vision Pro was doomed from the start. Despite its extraordinary capabilities, design flaws and a lack of apps at launch held it back significantly. But perhaps most damaging of all was its price. For $3,500, you'd expect the Vision Pro to do everything your MacBook does and more, but for many users, it became a glorified and overcomplicated external monitor. After an initial wave of hype, the Vision Pro faded away.

The Vision Pro got a single, half-hearted M5 enhancement in October 2025, but the writing was on the wall. Apple was already pulling staff from the project to focus on cheaper, more approachable smart glasses and, by June 2026, analyst Ming-Chi Kuo suggested that Apple had dropped its headset program entirely, leaving only a couple of smart glasses in development.

Industry observers note that but other VR and XR headsets have fared better, most notably the Meta Quest 2, which became the best-selling VR headset of all time, and its successor, the Quest 3. Why did Meta succeed enough to remain in the market while Apple failed despite releasing a polished first-generation product? The answer is twofold: Apple doesn't need the Vision Pro as much as Meta needed the Quest, and the Vision Pro sacrificed mainstream accessibility to meet Apple's notoriously rigid product standards.

When the Apple Vision Pro arrived, some analysts were astounded by its $3,500 price, a number that suggests Apple never intended it to become truly mainstream. Apple might be able to get away with charging $1,000 for an iPhone or $2,000 for an iPhone Duo (especially with carrier subsidies, deals and purchase plans), but more than triple that for a device that required consumers not only to learn an entirely fresh operating system in three dimensions but also to find a practical use for it in their daily lives? It was never going to tempt anyone beyond the wealthiest subset of Apple enthusiasts, especially since it lacked any killer apps at launch.

More charitable onlookers insisted Apple had a larger vision for the Vision Pro. The first generation was for developers, some said, and mass appeal would materialize as future headsets got cheaper and added more apps. But a classic chicken-and-egg problem emerged: no one wanted to develop for a platform with so few users, and few users wanted to buy into a platform with so few native apps. It's a tale as old as time, with products like the Windows Phone and Apple's own Newton PDA falling victim to the same dilemma.

It has been revealed that while Apple hasn't released concrete sales data for the Vision Pro, estimates generally put the figure at around or under 500,000 units. That's far below Apple's initial expectations and less than what such a complex, cutting-edge device would need to sell to make financial sense. Demand for a device that costs more than your mortgage payment and makes you look like you're wearing the world's dorkiest ski goggles was, as it turns out, not very high.

It has been revealed that despite the Meta Quest line's relative success, it hasn't really made VR and XR that popular. While the Quest 2 is widely considered the best-selling VR headset of all time, even the most generous estimates put sales at around 20 million units. By way of comparison, the Sony PlayStation 4 sold more than 100 million units, and Apple sold around 226 million iPhones in 2024 alone. Compared to sales numbers for popular tech products, VR's best-selling product barely registers. Its follow-up, the Quest 3, was even less impressive, only unseating the Quest 2 as the most popular headset on Steam in late 2026.

The Quest 2's figures can't be fully chalked up to consumer enthusiasm, either. Facebook poured over $80 billion into the so-called metaverse starting in 2021, even renaming itself to Meta as part of its effort to dominate what Mark Zuckerberg called the "next chapter for the internet." The Quest 2 was Meta's flagship headset at the time, so it makes sense it got more attention than other VR headsets. For his part, Zuckerberg could not have been more wrong and, while Meta has seen success with its AI-equipped Meta glasses, it has failed to move the needle on full-fat VR and XR headsets.

One warning sign for Apple in the lead-up to the Vision Pro's release should have been Meta's own high-end headset, the Quest Pro. Introduced in October 2022 for $1,500, the Quest Pro promised everything Meta couldn't afford to put in its budget-priced Quest 2: eye tracking, productivity software and better passthrough. It was an immediate flop, prompting Meta to slash $500 off the price about six months later before discontinuing it in 2024. In that context, it's no wonder Apple's $3,500 headset didn't fare much better.
